content: This includes achieving the goal of protecting one billion more people from emergencies and ensuring one billion more individuals experience improved health and well-being. The World Health Organization (WHO) is committed to providing more effective and efficient support to countries, focusing on universal health coverage (UHC), better protection indices, and healthier population indices. When developing a new Country Cooperation Strategy (CCS), it is never created from scratch but builds upon existing priorities and programs. Key steps include verifying alignment with national needs, assessing WHO’s comparative advantage in delivering priority areas, determining the contributions of other partners, identifying major gaps not addressed by WHO or other stakeholders, and highlighting opportunities for innovation or partnerships. The CCS process involves analyzing and mapping national priorities, reviewing alignment with previous strategies, and identifying gaps for dialogue. The strategy also incorporates national health and development priorities, partner projects, and capacities, including those of UN agencies. The six stages of the CCS cycle include identifying health challenges, gaps in outcomes, and priority interventions, as well as ensuring WHO’s comparative advantage in policy dialogue, technical assistance, and service delivery. Strategic priorities are jointly determined by the government and WHO, following the SMART criteria (specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, and time-bound). These priorities must align with GPW 13 outcomes and respond to the national health agenda. The prioritization process considers the type of support needed based on the country’s health system capacity and stability. For each agreed priority, clear expectations are set for WHO’s support at all levels, ensuring alignment with the organization’s working strategy. The CCS document is structured to include a cover page, signature page, executive summary, introduction, health and development situation, partnership environment, and strategic priorities. It outlines WHO’s collaboration with the country, including technical focus areas, contributions to regional and global health agendas, and implementation plans. The CCS also serves as an advocacy and planning tool to mobilize resources and foster strategic partnerships. The CCS launch is an opportunity to increase visibility and engagement, involving key stakeholders such as government officials, UN agencies, development partners, and civil society. Innovative ideas for the launch include media engagement, expert panels, social media campaigns, and public commitments to health goals. Monitoring and evaluation activities, including midterm and final evaluations, assess progress, identify challenges, and provide recommendations for future collaboration. The midterm evaluation focuses on tracking progress, identifying impediments, and adjusting priorities as needed. The final evaluation provides a comprehensive assessment of achievements, gaps, and lessons learned, feeding into the development of a new CCS. The evaluation process involves collaboration between WHO, the government, and other stakeholders, ensuring joint ownership of results. The CCS is a critical tool for guiding WHO’s collaboration with countries, supporting national health agendas, and contributing to global health goals.
